title: Insider cluster buys — what they are and why they matter
body_md:
Corporate insiders — officers, directors, and holders of more than 10% of a class of shares — must report their trades to the SEC on Form 4, generally within two business days of the transaction. That short lag is what makes insider data useful: it is close to real time by regulatory standards.

A single insider buying is weak evidence; people buy for many reasons. A **cluster** — several distinct insiders at the same company making open-market purchases in a short window — is stronger, because it is harder to explain away as one person's liquidity need. TradeOS scores only open-market purchases (transaction code P), because routine sales, option exercises, and tax-withholding sales carry little directional information. It counts distinct insiders as distinct voices, so one person filing many purchases cannot masquerade as a crowd.

title: Activist stakes — reading Schedule 13D
body_md:
An investor who acquires more than 5% of a company's voting shares and intends to influence control must file a **Schedule 13D** with the SEC, generally within a short window of crossing the threshold. Unlike the passive 13G, a 13D signals intent — a proxy fight, a board seat, a push for a sale or spin-off.

A 13D is one of the timeliest institutional disclosures available, which is why TradeOS weights a new activist stake highly. But timeliness is not certainty: a stake is a bet, not an outcome. TradeOS records the filer and the subject company from the machine-structured filing header and never scrapes a percentage from the free-form cover page, because a guessed number would be a fabricated one.

title: Passive >5% stakes — reading Schedule 13G
body_md:
**Schedule 13G** is the passive cousin of the 13D: it is filed by investors who cross 5% but do not intend to influence control — most often large index funds and asset managers. It carries less directional signal than a 13D because it often reflects mechanical index weighting rather than conviction.

TradeOS treats 13G as a weaker contributing voice, and — importantly — collapses an institution's 13G and any 13F holding on the same issuer into a single voice, because they are the same party. Counting one filer twice would manufacture false convergence.

title: 13F holdings — powerful, but read the delay
body_md:
Institutional managers over a size threshold report their U.S. equity holdings quarterly on **Form 13F**, and they may file up to 45 days after quarter-end. So a 13F you read today can describe positions that are already months old, and it shows longs only — not shorts, options, or non-U.S. holdings.

This staleness is the single most important thing to internalize about 13F. TradeOS stores two timestamps on every holding — the quarter-end it describes and the date it actually became public — and displays the gap, so a quarterly snapshot never masquerades as a live position. Because the demo has only one quarter, 13F is shown as context and not yet scored: 'new or increased position' is a quarter-over-quarter fact that a single snapshot cannot establish.

title: Short interest and days-to-cover
body_md:
FINRA publishes consolidated equity **short interest** twice a month — the aggregate number of shares sold short and not yet covered. Divided by average daily volume, it yields **days-to-cover**, a rough measure of how long it would take shorts to buy back their position.

Short interest is ambiguous on its own: a high figure can mean bearish conviction or fuel for a squeeze. It also arrives on a lag — settlement is mid- or end-of-month, publication about eight business days later. TradeOS shows the derived change and days-to-cover as corroborating context with that lag labeled, and does not (yet) weight it into the convergence score.

title: Why convergence beats any single signal
body_md:
Any one disclosure is noisy. An insider may buy for personal reasons; an activist may be wrong; a fund's quarterly snapshot may be stale. The idea behind convergence is that **independent** sources agreeing is much stronger evidence than any of them alone — the way separate witnesses telling the same story is more convincing than one witness repeating it.

The hard word is *independent*. Ten signals that all trace to one origin are one signal, not ten. TradeOS enforces this with an independence step: it groups events by the party behind them, counts each party's strongest event fully and its extras at a fraction, and requires several distinct parties across at least two different source types before it will publish a cluster. That is what prevents one actor — or one loud filer — from manufacturing a signal.

title: Base rates and calibration — the honest way to state confidence

sources.title: SEC — backtesting and performance disclosure principles

body_md:
A **base rate** is how often something has historically happened: of past clusters like this one, what fraction were followed by a positive excess return? A **calibrated** confidence means the stated probability matches reality — when a well-calibrated system says 70%, the event happens about 70% of the time.

Calibration is the whole game, and it is easy to fake with a small sample: a '100% hit rate' on three episodes is astrology. TradeOS refuses to state a rate on fewer than 30 resolved episodes, shows a confidence interval on every rate it does state, and labels its buckets 'backtested calibration pending' until enough live signals accrue. A base rate is a fact about a pattern's history — never a prediction about your position.

title: Survivorship and look-ahead bias — how backtests lie

sources.title: SEC — investor education on performance claims

body_md:
Two biases quietly inflate almost every naive backtest. **Survivorship bias** is testing only the companies that still exist, silently dropping the ones that failed — which makes any strategy look better than it was. **Look-ahead bias** is letting the test peek at information that was not yet public on the day it is pretending to trade.

TradeOS attacks both structurally. Its universe comes from who filed at the time, not from a current index, and names with no price history are counted and displayed as exclusions rather than dropped. And every signal is computed strictly through the moment each fact became publicly knowable, with a guard that discards anything not yet public — so a backtest can never trade on tomorrow's news.

title: Position sizing — the decision that isn't about being right
body_md:
How much to allocate to an idea is often more consequential than whether the idea is correct. Sizing too large means a normal losing streak can end the game; sizing too small means even good ideas barely matter. Diversification across independent bets reduces the chance that any single mistake is fatal.

This entry is educational and general. TradeOS describes what disclosed sources are doing and how patterns have historically behaved; it does not tell any user how much to buy, when, or whether to buy at all. Sizing is a personal decision that depends on circumstances the platform neither sees nor evaluates.

title: Risk management — surviving to compound

sources.title: SEC investor.gov — assessing your risk tolerance

body_md:
Compounding only works if you stay in the game, so avoiding ruin matters more than maximizing any single outcome. Common principles include limiting exposure to correlated bets (positions that fall together are not really diversified), planning for the case where a thesis is wrong, and remembering that leverage magnifies both the good and the fatal.

General and educational: nothing here is advice for a specific person. TradeOS provides transparent, probability-framed intelligence and an honest track record; what to do with it is the user's own decision.

title: How to read an SEC filing on EDGAR
body_md:
Every disclosure TradeOS uses is a public document on the SEC's EDGAR system, and you can verify any of them yourself. Each filing has a machine-structured header — accession number, acceptance datetime, the filer and (for 13D/G) the subject company with their CIKs — and a body. TradeOS relies on the header, which is authoritative, and treats the free-form body with care.

The single best habit for a skeptical user: pick a signal, open the underlying Form 4 or Schedule 13D on EDGAR, and confirm it. A platform that survives that check every time is trustworthy; one that doesn't isn't. Verifiability is the point.

title: Congressional trading disclosure — and its limits
body_md:
Under the STOCK Act, members of Congress must periodically disclose their securities transactions. In practice the data is messy: amounts are reported only as broad ranges, filings can arrive weeks after the trade, and the House often publishes scanned PDFs rather than structured data.

TradeOS keeps congressional trading as a modular, optional input that is currently off, because no clean, structured primary source is accessible without either scraping a bot-blocked portal or reading scanned PDFs — and guessing would violate the platform's honesty rules. It is built so it can be turned on the day a clean source exists, and the convergence signal is designed to work identically with it off.

title: Options flow — what unusual activity can and can't tell you
body_md:
Large or unusual options activity — sweeps of out-of-the-money calls, sudden jumps in open interest — is sometimes read as a footprint of informed positioning. It can be, but it is also easy to misread: options are used for hedging and income as often as for directional bets, and one large trade has a counterparty on the other side.

Options flow is on the TradeOS roadmap via a licensed data provider, shown today only as a clearly watermarked design preview with fictional tickers. It is not live data, and nothing in the preview is a measurement.

title: Market structure — liquidity, and why it matters for signals
body_md:
**Liquidity** — how easily a security can be traded without moving its price — shapes how much any signal is worth. In a thin, low-volume stock, a small amount of buying (or a fabricated filing) can move the price a lot, which is exactly why illiquid names are the cheapest to manipulate.

TradeOS applies a liquidity floor: clusters on names below the floor are pushed to low confidence and kept out of the default feed, visible only in the screener behind a manipulation-risk warning. This is a first line of defense against a signal being used as a pump instrument.

title: Warren Buffett — long-term ownership and margin of safety
body_md:
Draft profile for founder review. Across decades of publicly published Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters, Warren Buffett has described an approach centered on buying durable businesses at a sensible price and holding for the long term — treating a share as partial ownership of a business rather than a ticker to trade. He has publicly emphasized a 'margin of safety' (buying below a conservative estimate of value) and a preference for companies with lasting competitive advantages.

This is a neutral summary of positions Buffett has himself stated publicly; it invents no views and reproduces no copyrighted text. Berkshire's holdings are visible in its quarterly 13F filings — with the standard quarterly delay every 13F carries.

title: Peter Lynch — invest in what you understand

sources.title: Public interviews and lectures (various, publicly available)

body_md:
Draft profile for founder review. As the manager of a large U.S. mutual fund in the 1980s, Peter Lynch became widely associated with the idea of investing in businesses an ordinary person can understand, doing one's own research, and being patient. He has publicly discussed favoring companies whose products and economics are comprehensible over those that are fashionable but opaque.

This summary reflects positions Lynch has stated publicly in interviews and talks; it invents no views and reproduces no copyrighted material. It is educational context, not a recommendation.

title: Carl Icahn — activism and the 13D playbook
body_md:
Draft profile for founder review. Carl Icahn is among the best-known activist investors: he takes large stakes in public companies and pushes, often publicly, for changes he argues will raise shareholder value — board seats, spin-offs, buybacks, or a sale. The mechanics are visible in his Schedule 13D filings, which by rule disclose an intent to influence control.

This is a factual description of a public, filing-documented style of activism; it invents no views, makes no claim about any specific outcome, and reproduces no copyrighted material.

title: Michael Burry — contrarian, thesis-driven positioning
body_md:
Draft profile for founder review. Michael Burry is known for contrarian, deeply-researched positions taken against prevailing sentiment. His firm's disclosed U.S. equity positions appear in quarterly 13F filings, which — like all 13Fs — are a delayed, longs-only snapshot and do not reveal shorts, options, or timing within the quarter.

This entry describes what is publicly disclosed and cautions against over-reading a quarterly snapshot; it invents no views and reproduces no copyrighted text.

title: Benjamin Graham — the value-investing tradition
body_md:
Draft profile for founder review. Benjamin Graham is widely regarded as the intellectual founder of value investing: buying securities for less than a conservative estimate of their worth, insisting on a 'margin of safety,' and treating market swings as an opportunity rather than a guide. His framework — analyzing a business's fundamentals rather than following price momentum — influenced generations of investors.

This is an original summary of a widely-documented framework; it invents no views and reproduces no copyrighted book text, and is educational background for the disciplines TradeOS applies to data.

title: Joel Greenblatt — special situations and simple rules
body_md:
Draft profile for founder review. Joel Greenblatt is associated with special-situations investing (spin-offs, restructurings) and with the idea that a small number of sensible, disciplined rules — buying good businesses at cheap prices — can work if followed consistently and patiently, even though they underperform for stretches.

This summary reflects ideas Greenblatt has presented publicly; it invents no views and reproduces no copyrighted material, and is offered as educational context.
